ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The Kangaroo Hotel has 30 floors numbered from 1 to 30 and each floor has 20 rooms numbered from 1 to 20. The code to enter the room is formed by joining the floor number with the room number, in that order. But this code can be confusing, as shown in the picture. Note that the code 101 is not confusing, as it can only refer to floor 10 and room 1 and never to floor 1 and room 1, as it has the code 11. How many codes are confusing, including the one in the figure?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The picture shows a kangaroo holding a sign with the code 111. In the thought bubble, the code is interpreted in two ways: as room 1 on floor 11, or as room 11 on the 1st floor. This illustrates that 111 is a confusing code. Reasoning: The hotel has floors 1 to 30 and rooms 1 to 20. A code is made by concatenating the floor number followed by the room number, with no leading zeros. Classify by code length. Two-digit codes can only be split as one digit for the floor and one digit for the room, so they are not confusing. Four-digit codes, coming from a two-digit floor and a two-digit room, cannot be validly split another way: a one-digit/three-digit split gives an invalid room, and a three-digit/one-digit split gives an invalid floor. Therefore only three-digit codes can be confusing. Let a three-digit code be abc. It is confusing exactly when both splits are valid: a|bc and ab|c. For a|bc, a is a one-digit floor and bc must be a room from 10 to 20. For ab|c, ab must be a floor from 10 to 30 and c must be a one-digit room from 1 to 9. Since c must be 1 to 9, bc cannot be 10 or 20, so bc must be 11 to 19. Thus b = 1 and c has 9 choices. Also ab = a1 must be at most 30, so a can be 1 or 2. Therefore there are 2 × 9 = 18 confusing codes.

Use the text to know that floors are 1–30, rooms are 1–20, and codes are made by concatenating floor then room with no leading zeros. Then classify codes by length. Two-digit codes have only one possible split into one digit and one digit, so they are not confusing. Four-digit codes from two-digit floor and two-digit room cannot be split validly another way because a one-digit/three-digit or three-digit/one-digit split would give an invalid room or floor. Thus only three-digit codes can be confusing. Write a three-digit code as abc. It is confusing exactly when both splits a|bc and ab|c are valid: a is a one-digit floor, bc is a room from 10 to 20, ab is a floor from 10 to 30, and c is a one-digit room. method.method_draft: First describe the image: it illustrates that a single written code, 111, can belong to two different room assignments, namely floor 11 room 1 and floor 1 room 11. From the text, form two sets of all possible three-digit codes, since ambiguity must occur between a one-digit floor with a two-digit room and a two-digit floor with a one-digit room. Let A be codes from floors 1–9 and rooms 10–20, and let B be codes from floors 10–30 and rooms 1–9. A confusing code is exactly an element of A∩B. A code in A has form xmn where x is the floor digit and mn is a room number 10–20. A code in B has form pqy where pq is a floor number 10–30 and y is the room digit. For the same three digits to be in both sets, the last two digits must form a valid room 10–20 and the first two digits must form a valid floor 10–30. The last digit also has to be a one-digit room, so it is 1–9, not 0; hence the two-digit room must be 11–19. Therefore the middle digit is 1. The first two digits are then 11 or 21, since 31 would exceed floor 30. Thus the common codes are 111–119 and 211–219, giving 9+9=18.
